extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (applicants, prosecutors, owners, and litigators)
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying and addressing double patenting issues during patent prosecution and litigation — i.e., detecting identical or obvious-variant claims across patents/continuations and applying remedies such as terminal disclaimers or claim redrafting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory double patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Bars an inventor from having two patents with the same claim (or effectively identical claims); the prohibition arises from 35 U.S.C. § 101, which allows an inventor to 'obtain a patent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because it requires the same claim in two patents, statutory double patenting is relatively easy to avoid and is fairly uncommon; can typically be avoided by slightly changing the claimed subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness-type double patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Bars a patent claim that is obvious over a claim in another of the inventor’s patents; the prohibition arises from case-law doctrine created by judges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designed to prevent extending the life of a first patent by obtaining a second patent to an obvious variation, and to protect third parties from harassment by multiple patent owners covering the same invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal disclaimer as remedy for obviousness-type double patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: A terminal disclaimer can overcome an obviousness-type double patenting rejection by making the later patent expire at the same time as the reference (earlier) patent and by tying enforceability to common ownership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminal disclaimers are only available under certain circumstances: they cannot be used if the reference patent has expired, and they are ineffective if the asserted and reference patents are not commonly owned. A terminal disclaimer may be submitted during prosecution and, in limited circumstances, during litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation filings and claim-drafting risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuation applications that reuse the same description and drawings but assert different claims can produce separate patents whose claims may be the same as or obvious variants of claims in the parent or sibling patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should draft claims across continuations carefully to avoid obtaining multiple patents that claim the same subject matter or obvious variations. Different wording or rearranged claim features can mask similarities and lead to missed double patenting rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner may use prior patents and prior art in double patenting analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: While the specification/drawings of a patent are not treated as prior art, the PTO is allowed to consider the prior art and other patents when performing a double patenting analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An examiner can cite historical documents or prior art to justify that a modification (e.g., converting a free-standing clock into a wrist watch) would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill, supporting an obviousness-type double patenting rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission-of-features often renders a claim obvious over another
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that simply omits features of another claim will generally be considered obvious over that other claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Claim B1 omits the second hand present in claim A1; in general, omission of features is a common basis for obviousness-type double patenting rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership, assignment, and common-ownership constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Terminal disclaimer and some avoidance strategies require common ownership of the later and reference patents; if ownership differs (e.g., patents assigned to different entities or sold), terminal disclaimers may not be effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Situations such as an inventor changing employers or patents being sold can prevent filing an effective terminal disclaimer and allow an earlier patent owned by another to be used to invalidate a later claim for double patenting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-examiner inconsistency and differing terminology can hide double patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Different examiners (or different claim terminology) across family members can lead to missed obviousness-type double patenting rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large application families examined by different examiners may use dissimilar claim language; applicants should be mindful that different wording can obscure substantially similar claim scope and cause problems later in litigation or enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double patenting as an invalidity defense in litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: If an examiner allows a claim that is obvious over a claim of another patent, an accused infringer can assert obviousness-type double patenting to invalidate that claim in litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a patent relied upon would not qualify as prior art under § 102 (e.g., not published more than a year earlier), a claim in that patent can still be used to assert double patenting invalidity against a later claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of equivalents and functional similarity in claim comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing claims for double patenting, courts and examiners will consider whether different words describe equivalent or functionally similar features (e.g., 'spring' vs 'rubber band', 'gear' vs 'cog', 'housing' vs 'cabinet').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if one claim recites more detailed elements and another uses broader or different terminology, functional equivalence can lead to a finding of obviousness-type double patenting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing date and expiration timing effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Earlier-filed patents may expire earlier and can still be used to invalidate later patents via double patenting; timing of filing and issuance affects availability of remedies like terminal disclaimers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the example, patent C was filed earlier and expired before patents A/B; patent C's existence and expiration timing meant Tempus could not rely on a terminal disclaimer against C (since Tempus did not own C), and C could be used to invalidate the later claim B1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Always consider double patenting during prosecution and enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Double patenting raises numerous issues in various factual scenarios and should always be a consideration for a patent applicant, patent owner, or an accused infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because double patenting can be subtle and arise from terminology, continuations, ownership changes, or earlier-filed patents, proactive assessment and claim strategy are recommended throughout prosecution and when asserting patents.
